title: Cap. II: Scholastici — causes of election (moral works / use of grace); Rom. 9 overthrows
latin: Sed descendamus a Semipelagianis ad Scholasticos. Ex hisce nonnulli docent causam dari praedestinationis seu electionis, quatenus cadit super hunc hominem potius quam super illum. Atque hic quidam obtendunt opera bona moralia, quae antecedunt gratiam justificationis; alii, opera bona quae subsequuntur; alii praevisum bonum usum gratiae Divinae. Verum haud necesse est ut in hisce sententiis refellendis inhaeream, quae omnes unico illo Apostoli ictu prosternuntur Rom. ix. 11. Nondum natis pueris, cum nihil fecissent boni vel mali, ut propositum Dei secundum electionem maneret, non ex operibus, sed ex vocante, dictum est, &c.
pass_a: But let us descend from the Semipelagians unto the Scholastics. Out of these not a few teach that a cause is given of predestination or election, insofar as it falls upon this man rather than upon that. And here certain ones put forward good moral works which precede the grace of justification; others, good works which follow; others the foresight good use of Divine grace. But it is hardly necessary that I should linger in refuting these opinions, which all are overthrown by that one stroke of the Apostle, Rom. ix. 11. The children being not yet born, when they had done nothing good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth, it was said, &c. Key lemmas: Scholastici; causa praedestinationis/electionis; opera bona moralia ante/post justificationem; praevisus bonus usus gratiae; Rom. ix. 11 non ex operibus.
pass_b: Next, down from the Semipelagians to the Scholastics. Not a few of them teach that predestination — or election — has a cause insofar as it falls on this man rather than that. Some plead good moral works before justifying grace; others good works after it; others foresight of a good use of God's grace. I need not linger refuting these views: one blow from the Apostle flattens them all (Rom. 9:11) — the children not yet born, having done nothing good or evil, so that God's purpose according to election might stand, not from works but from the One who calls.

lemmas.gloss: good moral works (before / after justifying grace)
foresight of a good use of grace

title: Cap. II: three causes of the election-from-foresight error (pride, ignorance, curiosity)
latin: Jam si quis quaerat unde hoc, quod tanto consensu Pelagiani, Semipelagiani, Scholastici, aliique multi electionem ad gratiam & gloriam inniti volunt alicui rei quod sit penes nos habere vel non habere, facere vel non facere, facile est hujus erroris causas designare. Prima est, innata humano generi superbia & philautia, quae aegerrime patitur omnem gloriandi causam eripi hominibus. Altera, crassa inscitia & ignorantia corruptionis nostrae, & voluntatis sub jugo peccati captivatae. Tertia, quia posita quacunque causa electionis in nobis, facile expediuntur omnes illae difficultates, quas alioqui cogemur ad altitudinem quandam inscrutabilem referre; quod curiositati humanae rationis valde adversatur. Nam posita electione juxta praescientiam alicujus operis humani, si quaeratur cur unus gratiam recipiat, alius non, illico occurrit: Quia unus se disposuit per liberum arbitrium, alius non. Si quaeratur cur unus perseveret in gratia, alius non perseveret, in promptu est responsio, Quia scilicet unus vult perseverare, alter non vult. Denique, si quaeratur cur hic ante constitutionem mundi electus fuerit ad gloriam, ille non fuerit, solvitur hic nodus facillime; Quia Deus praevidit ab aeterno unum admissurum oblatam gratiam, & bene illa usurum, & ad extremum usque vitae ex libero suo arbitrio in gratia permansurum, alterum aut repulsurum ab initio, aut saltem ante obitum excussurum.
pass_a: Now if anyone should ask whence this comes, that with so great consent Pelagians, Semipelagians, Scholastics, and many others will have election unto grace and glory to rest upon some thing which it is in our power to have or not to have, to do or not to do, it is easy to mark out the causes of this error. The first is pride and self-love innate to the human race, which most grudgingly suffers every cause of boasting to be snatched away from men. The second, thick unskillfulness and ignorance of our corruption, and of the will captive under the yoke of sin. The third, because once any cause of election whatsoever is set in us, all those difficulties are easily dispatched which otherwise we are forced to refer unto a certain inscrutable height; which is greatly adverse to the curiosity of human reason. For once election is set according to foresight of some human work, if it be asked why one receives grace, another not, at once it meets us: Because one disposed himself by free choice, another not. If it be asked why one perseveres in grace, another does not persevere, the answer is ready: Because namely one wills to persevere, the other does not will. Finally, if it be asked why this one before the world's founding was elect unto glory, that one was not, this knot is most easily loosed; Because God foresaw from eternity that one would admit the offered grace, and use it well, and to the very end of life from his free choice remain in grace, the other either thrust it back from the start, or at least shake it off before death. Key lemmas: superbia & philautia; inscitia corruptionis; curiositas rationis; praescientia operis humani.
pass_b: Why do Pelagians, Semipelagians, Scholastics, and so many others agree that election to grace and glory rests on something in our power to have or do? The causes of the error are plain. First: pride and self-love native to the race, which hates having every ground of boasting torn away. Second: thick ignorance of our corruption and of the will captive under sin's yoke. Third: put any cause of election in us, and the hard questions that otherwise force us up to an unsearchable height are easily waved off — and human curiosity hates that height. Once election tracks foresight of some human act, ask why one gets grace and another does not: because one disposed himself by free choice, the other did not. Why one perseveres and another not: because one wills to persevere, the other will not. Why this one was elect to glory before the world, that one not: God foresaw from eternity that one would admit offered grace, use it well, and stay in it by free choice to life's end — the other reject it at once, or at least shake it off before death.

title: Cap. II: fourth cause (cruelty charge); leave old Scholastics — Pontificii & Arminians next
latin: Postrema causa, qua moti sunt quamplurimi ut nullam admitterent electionem, nisi praescientia nixam alicujus actus eliciendi ex potestate liberi arbitrii, hac mihi fuisse videtur, Quod tanquam necessarium postulatum praesumpserunt, quod est fallissimum, scilicet, Deum crudelem fore, nisi in cujusvis hominis potestate constituat ut salutem possit, quam in Adamo emisit, per seipsum recuperare. Sed missis veteribus Pelagianis & Scholasticis, congrediamur cum illis qui nostro hoc seculo perturbant Ecclesiam, dum veteres errores interpolare & sub novis verborum formulis obtrudere conantur. Atque primo agemus contra Pontificios quosdam, dein contra Arminianos: qui in hoc consentiunt, quod electionem nullam ad salutem admittunt nisi nixam praescientia actuum humanorum eliciendorum, ex libero arbitrio per gratiam praevento.
pass_a: The last cause, by which very many have been moved to admit no election unless propped on foresight of some act to be elicited from the power of free choice, seems to me to have been this: That they presumed as a necessary postulate what is most false, namely, that God would be cruel unless he should set it in every man's power that he be able to recover by himself the salvation which he lost in Adam. But the old Pelagians and Scholastics being dismissed, let us join battle with those who in this our age disturb the Church, while they try to refresh old errors and thrust them in under new formulas of words. And first we will deal against certain Pontificals, then against the Arminians: who in this agree, that they admit no election unto salvation unless propped on foresight of human acts to be elicited, from free choice prevented by grace. Key lemmas: postulatum fallissimum; Deus crudelis; Pontificii; Arminiani; praescientia actuum; gratia praeveniens.
pass_b: A last motive for many who will admit no election except one resting on foresight of some act free choice can elicit: they took as a necessary postulate what is utterly false — that God would be cruel unless he put it in every person's power to recover by himself the salvation lost in Adam. Leave the old Pelagians and Scholastics. Engage those who disturb the Church in our age by dressing old errors in new formulas. First certain Papal doctors, then the Arminians: both refuse any election to salvation that does not rest on foresight of human acts elicited from free choice, grace having gone before.

title: Cap. II: Vasquez enters — thesis: efficacious election from foresight merits
latin: In arenam primo prodeant Papistae: atque pro caeteris omnibus qui hanc sententiam sequuntur (nam ex sanioribus multi non sequuntur) loquatur Vasques: Qui hanc thesin multis argumentis stabilire conatur, in 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. Nulla est electio efficax singularium personarum ad gloriam ex sola Dei voluntate; sed quilibet ad gloriam eligitur ex meritis praevisis, quae Dei gratia est facturus. Pauca praemitto, ut ipsa thesis melius intelligatur, dein argumenta adversariorum proponam & dissolvam.
pass_a: Into the arena first let the Papists come forth: and for all the rest who follow this opinion (for of the sounder ones many do not follow) let Vasquez speak: Who tries to establish this thesis with many arguments, in 1. quest. 23. art. 3. disp. 89. There is no efficacious election of singular persons unto glory from the sole will of God; but each one is elect unto glory from foresight merits, which by God's grace he is about to do. I premise a few things, that the thesis itself may be better understood; then I will set forth and dissolve the adversaries' arguments. Key lemmas: Papistae / Vasques; electio efficax; merita praevisa; 1. q. 23. a. 3. d. 89.
pass_b: First into the arena: the Papists. For all who hold this view (many of the sounder sort do not), let Vasquez speak. He tries to prop this thesis with many arguments (on ST 1.23.3, disp. 89): There is no efficacious election of particular persons to glory from God's will alone; each is elect to glory from foresight merits which God's grace will bring about. A few notes first so the thesis is clear; then the adversaries' arguments, stated and dissolved.

lemmas.gloss: ST I q.23 a.3, Vazquez disp. 89

title: Cap. II: Vasquez clarified — efficient election, merits as ratio, special grace vs Arminians
latin: Primo, per electionem efficacem videtur Vasques designare absolutam & peculiarem Dei voluntatem quae ad singulares & certas personas certo beandas terminatur, puta ad Petrum & Paulum reliquosque electos sigillatim. Hanc autem vocat efficacem electionem, vel efficacem voluntatem dandi gloriam, ut distinguatur ab illa communi & antecedente voluntate, sive simplici desiderio, aut affectu, quo statuunt Deum velle omnibus communicare etiam ipsis reprobis, vitam aeternam. Secundo, quando affirmat ex meritis praevisis esse hanc efficacem electionem ad gloriam, non illud vult, praevisa merita humana esse causam ipsius volitionis Divinae, cujus nulla causa extra Deum quaerenda est; sed esse rationem propter quam Divina voluntas libere terminetur ad hanc personam glorificandam. Tertio, quando addit, quae Dei gratia facturus est, vult suam sententiam a Pelagianis sejungere, qui merita, sive bona opera, ex libero arbitrio dimanare putabant absque illa gratia Christi, quam passim Augustinus ex sacris Scripturis esse necessariam demonstravit. Postremo, animadvertendum est, quamvis Jesuita tueatur, electionem efficacem ad gloriam non esse, nisi ex praevisione meritorum; lubenter tamen eundem concedere praedestinationem ad gratiam specialem, quae infallibiliter ducit ad gloriam, nulla niti praevisione meritorum, neque ex parte praedestinati excogitari posse ullam causam, ullum initium, ullam occasionem, cur Deus illi talem gratiam donaverit, aut in praescientia dare decreverit: Part. 1. quaest. 23. disp. 91. cap. 11. Hac igitur ex parte, de praedestinatione singularium personarum ad gratiam specialem multo rectius sentit Jesuita quam qui ex Schola Arminiana & Vorstiana prodierunt. Sed jam quibus argumentis praedictam thesin adstruant, dispiciamus. A Scripturis auspicantur, atque inde haec testimonia afferre solent pro electione ex praevisis operibus.
pass_a: First, by efficacious election Vasquez seems to designate an absolute and peculiar will of God which terminates upon singular and certain persons to be certainly blessed, for instance upon Peter and Paul and the remaining elect one by one. This moreover he calls efficacious election, or an efficacious will of giving glory, that it may be distinguished from that common and antecedent will, or simple desire, or affection, by which they hold that God wills to communicate eternal life to all, even to the reprobate themselves. Secondly, when he affirms that this efficacious election unto glory is from foresight merits, he does not mean that foresight human merits are the cause of the Divine volition itself, whose no cause outside God is to be sought; but that they are the reason on account of which the Divine will is freely terminated unto glorifying this person. Thirdly, when he adds, which by God's grace he is about to do, he wishes to sever his opinion from the Pelagians, who thought merits, or good works, to flow from free choice without that grace of Christ which Augustine everywhere demonstrated from the sacred Scriptures to be necessary. Lastly, it is to be noted that although the Jesuit maintains efficacious election unto glory not to be except from foresight of merits, yet the same gladly grants that predestination unto special grace, which infallibly leads unto glory, rests on no foresight of merits, nor can any cause, any beginning, any occasion be invented on the predestinate's part why God should have given him such grace, or decreed in foresight to give it: Part. 1. quest. 23. disp. 91. cap. 11. On this side, then, concerning predestination of singular persons unto special grace the Jesuit thinks far more rightly than those who have come forth from the Arminian and Vorstian School. But now let us look by what arguments they build up the aforesaid thesis. They begin from the Scriptures, and thence are wont to bring these testimonies for election from foresight works. Key lemmas: voluntas efficax / communis; ratio (non causa) volitionis; gratia specialis; Schola Arminiana & Vorstiana.
pass_b: First: by efficacious election Vasquez means God's absolute, particular will that settles on certain persons to be blessed — Peter, Paul, and the rest one by one. He calls it efficacious election, or an efficacious will to give glory, to mark it off from the common antecedent will (a bare desire or affection) by which they say God wills eternal life for all, even the reprobate. Second: when he says this efficacious election to glory is from foresight merits, he does not make those merits the cause of God's willing — no cause of that is sought outside God — but the reason why the divine will freely terminates on glorifying this person. Third: adding "which God's grace will bring about" cuts him off from Pelagians who let merits flow from free choice without Christ's grace, which Augustine everywhere proved from Scripture necessary. Last: though the Jesuit holds there is no efficacious election to glory except from foresight of merits, he gladly grants predestination to special grace that infallibly leads to glory rests on no foresight of merits, and no cause, start, or occasion can be invented on the predestinate's side why God gave that grace or decreed in foresight to give it (ST I q.23, disp. 91.11). On predestination of particular persons to special grace, then, the Jesuit is far sounder than the Arminian and Vorstian school. Now their arguments for the thesis: they start from Scripture and usually cite these for election from foresight works.

lemmas.gloss: merits as reason, not cause, of God's willing

title: Cap. II Arg. 1: Vasquez from Matt. 25:34 — kingdom prepared for foresight works
latin: Primo, Ex illis verbis Matth. xxv. 34, &c. Venite benedicti Patris, possidete regnum paratum vobis ab initio mundi. Esurivi enim, & dedistis mihi, &c. sic argumentatur Vasques, Hoc in loco Christus offert regnum praeparatum ab origine mundi, id est, ab aeternitate; atque reddit simul rationem cur debeant accipere praeparatum & destinatum, quod est causam ipsius praeparationis indicare. Nam si praeparatio sit alia ratione, & non propter haec ipsa opera quae nominantur, inanis & nulla plane esset causa quam hic ipse Christus assignavit. Ergo homines eliguntur ad gloriam caelestem ex praevisione operum suorum bonorum. In 1. quaest. 23. art. 3. cap. 2. disp. 89.
pass_a: First, From those words Matt. xxv. 34, &c. Come, ye blessed of the Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world. For I was hungry, and ye gave me, &c. thus Vasquez argues: In this place Christ offers the kingdom prepared from the world's origin, that is, from eternity; and at the same time he renders the reason why they ought to receive the prepared and destined, which is to indicate the cause of the preparation itself. For if the preparation be by another reason, and not on account of these very works which are named, empty and plainly none would be the cause which here Christ himself assigned. Therefore men are elect unto heavenly glory from foresight of their good works. In 1. quest. 23. art. 3. cap. 2. disp. 89. Key lemmas: Matth. xxv. 34; regnum paratum ab initio mundi; causa praeparationis; praevisio operum.
pass_b: First argument (Matt. 25:34ff.): "Come, you blessed of the Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the world's beginning. For I was hungry, and you gave me…" Vasquez: here Christ offers a kingdom prepared from the world's origin — that is, from eternity — and at once gives the reason they should receive what was prepared and destined, which is to mark the cause of that preparation. If the preparation rested on some other ground, and not on these very works named, the cause Christ himself assigns would be empty and none. Therefore people are elect to heavenly glory from foresight of their good works (ST I q.23 a.3, disp. 89.2).

lemmas.gloss: kingdom prepared from the world's beginning

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 1: works path to glory, not cause of decree — Scotus & Bellarmine
latin: Ex his verbis nihil aliud colligi potest, quam Dei filios, ab aeterno ad gloriam gratis praedestinatos, tandem illud adire, vel in illud intromitti, exclusis aliis, quia hi soli per rectam & a Deo ordinatam viam eo perrexerunt. Quod autem Vasques urget praedicta opera hoc in loco nominari ut causas ipsius praeparationis, sive aeternae destinationis Divinae, falsissimum est. Nam vera causa innuitur, quando benedicti Patris appellantur. Ideo siquidem haereditati caelesti illos destinavit quia ex gratia sua voluit effici illorum Pater in Christo. Opera autem illorum, neque ut praevisa, neque ut in tempore facta, erant causa praedestinationis ad gloriam, sed introductionis: neque hujus sunt causae meritoriae, sed causae solummodo subordinatae, eodem sensu quo motus in via causa dicitur perveniendi ad terminum viae. In hoc igitur lapsus est Vasques, quod non animadvertit, actum decernendi vel praedestinandi ad gloriam posse esse mere gratuitum in Deo, & nulla niti praevisione actuum humanorum: cum tamen modus perveniendi ad gloriam quoad hominem sit laboriosus, & requirat multos actus, sine quibus Deus ordinavit ac praevidit illum ad gloriae regnum nunquam appulsurum. Scotus hanc solutionem indicavit Lib. 1. dist. 41. ubi scribit, hanc propositionem, DEUS VULT PETRO DARE AETERNAM GLORIAM PROPTER MERITA, esse falsam, si illa verba, PROPTER MERITA, construantur cum verbo, VULT: non enim Deus ex praevisione meritorum concepit voluntatem glorificandi Petrum. Esse veram, si construantur cum verbo, DARE: non enim vult introducere in possessionem gloriae, nisi postquam praevisum est ambulasse in illis bonis operibus, quae Deus illi praescripsit & praeordinavit. Bellarminus eadem responsione utitur lib. 2. De grat. & libero arb. cap. 13. Haec propositio, DEUS AB AETERNO PRAEDESTINAVIT HOMINIBUS DARE REGNUM PER BONA OPERA PRAEVISA, potest & vera esse & falsa. Nam si illud, PER OPERA PRAEVISA, referatur ad verbum, PRAEDESTINAVIT, falsa erit: significabit enim Deum praedestinasse homines, quia opera illorum bona praeviderat; Si referatur ad verbum, DARE, vera erit: quia significabit glorificationem in exsecutione, esse effectum justificationis & sanctificationis sive operum bonorum. Sed hoc argumentum rursus urgebitur, & aliquanto fortius; ubi nos etiam plenius respondebimus.
pass_a: From these words nothing else can be gathered than that the sons of God, freely predestinated from eternity unto glory, at length approach that, or are let into it, others being shut out, because these alone by the right way ordained by God have proceeded thither. But what Vasquez presses — that the aforesaid works are named in this place as causes of the preparation itself, or of the eternal Divine destination — is most false. For the true cause is hinted when they are called blessed of the Father. Therefore indeed he destined them to the heavenly inheritance because from his grace he willed to be made their Father in Christ. But their works, neither as foresight nor as done in time, were the cause of predestination unto glory, but of introduction: nor of this are they meritorious causes, but causes only subordinate, in the same sense in which motion on the way is called a cause of arriving at the way's end. In this therefore Vasquez has slipped, that he has not noticed that the act of decreeing or predestinating unto glory can be merely gratuitous in God, and rest on no foresight of human acts: while yet the manner of arriving at glory as to man is laborious, and requires many acts, without which God has ordained and foresaw that he would never put in to the kingdom of glory. Scotus indicated this solution, Lib. 1. dist. 41, where he writes that this proposition, GOD WILLS TO GIVE PETER ETERNAL GLORY ON ACCOUNT OF MERITS, is false, if those words, ON ACCOUNT OF MERITS, be construed with the verb, WILLS: for God did not from foresight of merits conceive the will of glorifying Peter. It is true, if they be construed with the verb, TO GIVE: for he does not will to introduce into possession of glory except after it has been foresight that he walked in those good works which God prescribed and preordained for him. Bellarmine uses the same reply, book 2, On grace and free choice, chapter 13. This proposition, GOD FROM ETERNITY PREDESTINED TO GIVE MEN THE KINGDOM THROUGH FORESIGHT GOOD WORKS, can be both true and false. For if that, THROUGH FORESIGHT WORKS, be referred to the verb, PREDESTINED, it will be false: for it will signify that God predestined men because he had foresight their good works; If it be referred to the verb, TO GIVE, it will be true: because it will signify glorification in execution to be the effect of justification and sanctification or of good works. But this argument will be pressed again, and somewhat more strongly; where we also will answer more fully. Key lemmas: causa introductionis (non praedestinationis); Scotus dist. 41; Bellarminus De grat. 2.13; PROPTER MERITA with VULT vs DARE.
pass_b: From these words you may gather only this: God's children, freely predestined from eternity to glory, at last enter it — others shut out — because they alone took the straight road God ordained. Vasquez's claim that the works named here are causes of the preparation itself, or of God's eternal destination, is utterly false. The true cause is hinted when they are called the Father's blessed: he destined them to the heavenly inheritance because by grace he willed to be their Father in Christ. Their works, neither as foresight nor as done in time, caused predestination to glory — only introduction into it; and even of that they are not meritorious causes, only subordinate ones, as motion on a road is a "cause" of reaching the end. Vasquez's slip: he missed that decreeing or predestining to glory can be purely gratuitous in God and rest on no foresight of human acts, while the way of arriving at glory for man is laborious and needs many acts without which God ordained and foresaw he would never put in to glory's kingdom. Scotus (I dist. 41) marks the solution: "God wills to give Peter eternal glory on account of merits" is false if "on account of merits" construes with "wills" — God did not form the will to glorify Peter from foresight of merits — and true if it construes with "to give": he will not bring into possession of glory until it is foresight that Peter walked in the good works God prescribed and preordained. Bellarmine uses the same reply (De grat. et lib. arb. 2.13): "God from eternity predestined to give men the kingdom through foresight good works" is false if "through foresight works" hangs on "predestined," true if it hangs on "to give" — glorification in execution as the effect of justification, sanctification, or good works. This argument will be pressed again, harder; we will answer more fully then.

lemmas.gloss: cause of introduction (not of the decree)
Scotus on PROPTER MERITA with VULT vs DARE
